subject: Civil Engineering
title: Cantilever Beams: The Bold Reach
description: One-minute skill: Cantilever Beams: The Bold Reach.

hook.text: A diving board sticks out over nothing. One end is fixed, the other is free.

buildup.text: A cantilever beam is supported at only one end. The fixed end resists all forces.

discovery.text: The maximum bending moment sits at the fixed end — that joint takes the beating.

twist.text: Cantilevers let architects create dramatic overhangs without visible supports.

climax.text: Fallingwater's balconies cantilever over a waterfall — bold engineering and art.

punchline.text: One strong anchor lets a beam reach into thin air.

quiz.question: Where does the maximum bending moment occur in a cantilever beam?
options: At the free end where the load hangs
Exactly at the midpoint of the beam

details.summary: A cantilever beam is fixed at one end and free at the other, projecting outward without support at its tip. It develops maximum bending moment and shear at the fixed support, the opposite of a simply supported beam.
details.whyItMatters: Cantilever construction enables dramatic architectural features and practical bridge-building techniques. Understanding the inverted moment distribution is essential because the tension side flips compared to simply supported beams.
takeaways: Maximum bending moment occurs at the fixed support end, not at midspan
The top face of a cantilever is in tension, opposite to a simply supported beam
Cantilever bridge construction extends from both sides simultaneously toward midspan

faq.question: Why is the bending moment distribution reversed in a cantilever compared to a simply supported beam?
faq.answer: In a simply supported beam, sagging creates compression on top and tension on bottom, with maximum moment at midspan. A cantilever hogging creates tension on top and compression on bottom, with maximum moment at the fixed support where the load effect is greatest.

faq.question: How does cantilever construction work for large bridges?
faq.answer: Bridge segments are built from each pier extending outward in both directions simultaneously, with temporary counterweights or cables providing balance. The growing arms eventually meet at midspan where a closing segment connects them.
